presets.label: Comfortable baseline
presets.summary: A modest AI payload with reasonably sized hardware in low Earth orbit. Both budgets have headroom.
presets.explanation: A 250 W compute request against a 3 m² radiator and a 6 m² solar array in the default idealized 600 km dawn-dusk orbit. The model’s fixed Sun geometry gives this orbit 100% sunlight; seasonal Sun motion and J2 precession are not simulated. This uses about 18% of the thermal budget and about 17% of the power budget, and is comfortably Safe on both counts. It is the reference point for the scenarios that follow, each of which changes one specific thing about this baseline to break it in an identifiable way.

assumptions: Steady state only for the thermal balance. There is no thermal mass and no transient temperature response, so a given moment is either thermally sustainable indefinitely or it is not.

The electrical power balance is averaged over a full orbit using the orbit’s eclipse duty cycle, but still holds no battery state of charge. It answers whether a continuous load is sustainable on average across an orbit, not whether it can run through eclipse itself without a battery, and not through an extended eclipse season.
The Sun direction used for both the eclipse and the solar array tracking calculations is a single fixed vector, not tied to any real epoch, season or beta angle.

The eclipse duty cycle uses the standard cylindrical-shadow approximation (an infinite shadow cylinder of Earth’s radius), ignoring the penumbra and Earth’s finite angular size as seen from the satellite.
The Earth view factor is supplied as an input rather than derived from radiator geometry and attitude during flight.

The coolant loop is single-phase, using a space-grade dielectric fluid such as Galden PFPE with a fixed specific heat of 1050 J/kg·K, rather than water or a water-glycol mixture, which would not survive deep-space eclipse temperatures and would pose a short-circuit risk near dense electronics. There is no two-phase behaviour and no pump power cost, and the transport figure represents the heat the loop can move while keeping the payload under its maximum allowable temperature, not a hard physical ceiling.

Parasitic heat is reused as a proxy for non-compute bus electrical draw, on the basis that electrical power in and waste heat out are close for resistive and electronic loads. It excludes power radiated away directly, such as by an RF payload, or diverted to active heaters, for which that equivalence does not hold.
Compute electrical power is assumed to convert entirely to waste heat.
Radiator temperature is uniform, with no gradients, conduction paths or multi-node spacecraft network.

Surfaces are modelled as ideal selective surfaces: constant solar absorptivity in the ultraviolet and visible band, and constant thermal emissivity in the infrared band, each independent of the other. This is standard practice for spacecraft thermal coatings and is not the same as a true grey body, which requires the two to be equal.

presets.label: Oversized payload in GEO
presets.summary: A large AI payload placed in a geostationary orbit with only modest hardware. It fails on both budgets.
presets.explanation: This moves to geostationary altitude and requests 2,500 W of compute while keeping the radiator and array close to the baseline size. Earth’s view factor drops to near zero out here, which helps the thermal side a little, and this orbit happens to show no eclipse at all against this tool’s fixed Sun direction, which helps the power side. Neither comes close to compensating for a tenfold increase in compute on similarly sized hardware: the result is about 167% of the thermal budget and about 113% of the power budget, Overheating on both counts. The lesson is that changing orbit is not a substitute for sizing the radiator and array to the actual compute load, and the compute request is almost always the dominant lever.

presets.label: Power-limited, not heat-limited
presets.summary: Plenty of radiator but a small solar array. The bottleneck is generating electricity rather than shedding heat.
presets.explanation: A generous 10 m² radiator handles 900 W of compute heat easily, using only 16% of the thermal budget. A small, inefficient and poorly pointed 1.5 m² array generates only about 240 W even in full sunlight. The 900 W request plus bus overhead comes to about 392% of available power, so the status reads Overheating for an electrical reason rather than a thermal one. The status badge alone cannot tell you this: you have to look at the telemetry bar and notice that the thermal figure shows headroom while the power figure shows a large deficit. This is why the tool tracks the two budgets separately instead of folding them into a single number.

presets.label: Heat-limited, not power-limited
presets.summary: Plenty of solar power but a tiny, poorly oriented radiator. The bottleneck is shedding heat rather than generating power.
presets.explanation: The mirror image of the previous scenario, using the same 900 W compute request so the two can be compared directly. The array here is generous at 14 m² and well pointed, generating far more power than needed, at about 18% power utilisation. The radiator, however, is only 1 m², has poor emissivity, absorbs sunlight readily and sits nearly face-on to the Sun, so it can reject only about 35 W net. The 900 W request is roughly 26 times that figure, so the configuration is heavily Overheating for purely thermal reasons. In practice a radiator this undersized would need to be far larger, angled away from the Sun, or paired with a drastically throttled compute load.

presets.label: The instantaneous-power trap
presets.summary: Looks comfortably fine if you only check full-sun generation. The real, eclipse-averaged figure says otherwise.
presets.explanation: A 600 W compute request against a 2.4 m² array in an orbit that is sunlit about 61% of the time. Checked against the array’s instantaneous full-sun output alone, the load uses about 70% of that supply, which reads as comfortable Margin and nothing to worry about. But a continuous compute load has to be sustained across the whole orbit, including the roughly 39% spent in Earth’s shadow, and the array only generates that instantaneous figure while it is actually sunlit. Averaged correctly over the full orbit, the same load comes to about 115% of what the array actually supplies: Overheating on the power budget, despite looking fine by the naive check. This is the exact trap an instantaneous-only power comparison sets: it implicitly assumes 100% duty cycle sunlight, which no real orbit gives you without a battery to carry the load through eclipse, and this tool does not model one.

presets.label: Transport-limited monolithic node
presets.summary: A large radiator on a thin coolant loop. Most of the radiating capacity sits idle because the loop cannot deliver the heat to it.
presets.explanation: A 15 m² radiator at 80 °C could reject about 9,295 W net of solar, albedo and parasitic loads, but the coolant loop (0.05 kg/s with a 5 K rise) can move only about 263 W to it. The 2,000 W request is therefore about 762% of the usable thermal budget and the status reads Overheating, even though roughly 9,030 W of radiating capacity (about 97% of it) goes unused. Power is not the problem: in the default eclipse-free orbit the 30 m² array supplies about 8.44 kW against a 2.03 kW bus load. This is what happens when radiator area keeps growing on a single node without growing the loop that feeds it: the binding limit stops being radiation and becomes plumbing. Raising the flow to 0.2 kg/s at a 10 K rise (about 2,100 W) lifts the ceiling above the request. In this tool the transport figure is a design limit rather than a physical wall, but it grows only as fast as the loop does, which is one reason large platforms split their heat across many loops and one reason fleets of smaller nodes are attractive.

diagnostics.message: Coolant transport capacity is the limiting factor. Increase the flow rate or the allowable coolant temperature rise.

presets.label: Tiny node overhead (micro-swarm)
presets.summary: A 100 W node carrying 30 W of fixed avionics heat. The fixed tax is a large slice of a small radiator’s budget.
presets.explanation: A 100 W compute request on a 1 m² radiator at 65 °C, with 30 W of avionics and housekeeping heat that does not shrink just because the node does. The heat budget before parasitics is about 526 W, so the fixed 30 W takes about 5.7% of that budget (and equals 30% of the compute heat itself). The node is comfortably Safe, at about 20% of the thermal budget and about 31% of the power budget on a 1.5 m² array. The point is the overhead: at this size a large share of every radiator and array watt is spent keeping the node alive rather than computing, which is why swarms of very small nodes are an expensive way to buy a given amount of compute. Compare the next preset, which has the same flux per square metre.

presets.label: Scaled node overhead (modular fleet)
presets.summary: The same 30 W of fixed heat on a 1 kW node. Same flux per square metre, but the overhead share falls by about eight times.
presets.explanation: The previous preset scaled up: 1,000 W of compute on an 8 m² radiator, at the same 65 °C, the same environment and the same 30 W of fixed parasitic heat. Gross radiator flux is identical at about 565 W/m², so the area needed per watt of heat has not changed, which is the fleet-invariance point in Study 01: dividing a heat load between nodes does not change the total radiator area, only the overhead. Net of solar and albedo loads the radiator can reject about 4,206 W before parasitics, so the same 30 W is about 0.7% of that budget, down from 5.7%, and 3% of compute heat instead of 30%. The status is Safe at about 24% of the thermal budget and about 37% of power budget on a 10 m² array. Beyond this size the overhead is already small, so further scaling buys little, while the loop and packaging demands shown in the transport-limited preset keep growing with the node.

presets.label: Fleet Node (175 kW class)
presets.summary: One modular 175 kW-class node. A fleet of about 28,600 such nodes aggregates to 5 GW without changing flux per square metre.
presets.explanation: Representative 175 kW fleet node. Reported AI1 figures range from 120 kW average (Musk/SpaceX) to 175 kW average (one outlet); Starcloud-3 is described as ~200 kW. This representative 160 m² dual-sided radiator model runs at 122 °C, with a 1,050 m² solar array. The 600 km high-beta dawn-dusk-like SSO setting is an idealized model assumption, not a stated orbit; this fixed-Sun orientation is eclipse-free in the model, which does not simulate seasonal Sun motion or J2 precession. Net thermal capacity is about 178.7 kW (radiator flux about 1,158 W/m²), so the 175 kW request sits at 97.9% thermal utilisation, deliberately close to its ceiling. The array generates about 295.4 kW against the 177.5 kW electrical load, for about 60.1% power utilisation and 117.9 kW of headroom. Overall status reads Limit, driven by thermal capacity. Because radiator flux depends only on temperature, emissivity and view factor, not node size, about 28,600 identical nodes (5 GW / 175 kW) reach the same 5 GW aggregate as the Monolith preset while keeping each node’s coolant loop and packaging inside ordinary single-loop limits. Compare directly with the Monolith (5 GW Concept) preset below.

presets.label: Monolith (5 GW Concept)
presets.summary: A single multi-km platform aggregating 5 GW of compute heat across massive parallel coolant loops and radiator panels.
presets.explanation: The original Starcloud-style monolithic concept: 5 GW of continuous compute on one platform, with 1e7 m² of two-sided radiator (order of a few kilometres on a side) at 75 °C, and an aggregate coolant flow of 320,000 kg/s standing in for many parallel loops rather than one physically continuous pipe. The 600 km high-beta dawn-dusk-like SSO setting is an idealized model assumption, not a stated concept-design parameter; this fixed-Sun orientation is eclipse-free in the model, which does not simulate seasonal Sun motion or J2 precession. Net thermal capacity is about 6.47 GW (radiator flux about 672 W/m²), so 5 GW sits at 77.3% thermal utilisation, with roughly 1.47 GW of headroom. Transport capacity (6.72 GW) exceeds net radiative capacity, so radiation, not plumbing, is the binding limit. The 3e7 m² array generates about 8.439 GW against a 5.002 GW bus load, for 59.3% power utilisation and about 3.437 GW of headroom. Overall status is Margin; neither budget is exceeded. The aggregate flow is a model abstraction for many parallel loops, not a claim that one physical pipe carries that flow. Compare directly with Fleet Node (175 kW class) above: same aggregate 5 GW, similar thermal headroom, radically different plumbing.
